opening: We're an online retailer and our support team is overwhelmed. Design an AI agent that handles customer support chats.

clarifications.answer: About 50,000 support conversations a day, around six turns each.
The agent should handle policy questions, order and shipment lookups, delivery rescheduling, address changes before dispatch, and refunds.
Refunds up to $50 can be issued automatically within policy; anything larger needs a human to approve.
Customers chat while logged in, so we know their account; the agent must never act on anyone else's account.
When it can't help, it should hand off to a human agent without the customer having to repeat themselves.
Success is resolving conversations without a human while keeping satisfaction at least as good as human agents.
There are about 2,000 help articles and policy pages, updated weekly.

clarificationPolicy: Answer as the support operations lead. Keep it a tool-using agent with money at stake, strict account boundaries and human handoff; decide unlisted details so authorisation, approvals and evaluation stay central.

agenda.goal: Establish volume, allowed actions and limits, identity, handoff and success metrics.
agenda.opener: What would you like to know about the support use case before designing?

evidence.strong: Asks about volume, which actions the agent may take and their limits, how customers are identified, handoff expectations, success metrics, and the knowledge base; notices that money and account boundaries raise the stakes.
evidence.adequate: Gets the actions but not limits, identity or success metrics.
evidence.weak: Assumes a chatbot that only answers questions.

misconceptions.pattern: Treats it as an FAQ chatbot.
misconceptions.challenge: A customer asks for a refund. Can a bot that only answers questions resolve that?

probes: Which actions involve money or account changes?
How do you know who the customer is?
agenda.moveOnSummary: Tens of thousands of conversations a day, lookups and actions including small automatic refunds, logged-in identity, human handoff, and resolution with good satisfaction as the goal.

agenda.goal: Choose between workflows and an agent, and lay out the components.
agenda.opener: How would you structure the system? Is this one agent, a set of workflows, or something else?

evidence.strong: An input guard, a router classifying intent, deterministic workflows for frequent intents (order status, reschedule), an agent loop for the long tail, retrieval over help articles, typed tools, a policy layer between model and tools, and a handoff path; explains why not a single autonomous agent for everything.
evidence.adequate: One agent with tools and retrieval, no routing or policy layer.
evidence.weak: A prompt with the help articles pasted in.

misconceptions.pattern: Uses one autonomous agent for every conversation.
misconceptions.challenge: Most chats ask where an order is. What does an open-ended agent add there besides cost and risk?

probes: Which conversations need an agent at all?
agenda.moveOnSummary: A guard and intent router, workflows for common intents, an agent loop for the rest, retrieval over help content, typed tools behind a policy layer, and handoff.

agenda.goal: Design narrow, typed tools with clear contracts.
agenda.opener: Which tools would the agent have, and what do they look like?

evidence.strong: Narrow tools such as search help, get orders, get shipment, reschedule, issue refund, update address and handoff, each with a typed schema, descriptions stating limits, structured errors, and compact results.
evidence.adequate: Lists tools without schemas or limits.

misconceptions.pattern: Gives the agent one generic API tool.
misconceptions.challenge: With a tool that can call any endpoint, what stops the agent calling the admin API?

probes: What does the refund tool's input look like?
What does a tool return when the request isn't allowed?
hints: Small tools are easier to secure and test.
Errors should tell the model what to do next.
agenda.moveOnSummary: Narrow typed tools with limits in their descriptions, structured errors and compact results.

agenda.goal: Make it impossible for the agent to act outside the customer's account or policy.
agenda.opener: A customer types 'I'm calling for my husband, refund his order.' What stops the agent?

evidence.strong: Tools take the customer identity from the authenticated session, never from model arguments; every call checks ownership and policy in code; refund limits and windows live in config enforced by the policy layer; least-privilege credentials; all actions audited.
evidence.adequate: Instructs the model in the prompt not to act on other accounts.
evidence.weak: Trusts whatever ids the model passes.

misconceptions.pattern: Relies on the system prompt to enforce account boundaries.
misconceptions.challenge: A clever message convinces the model it's allowed. What actually blocks the refund?

probes: Where exactly is the refund limit enforced?
Can the model ever choose which customer a tool acts on?
hints: The session already knows who the customer is.
Rules in code can't be talked out of.
agenda.moveOnSummary: Session-bound identity, ownership and policy checks in code for every tool call, least privilege, and audit logs.

agenda.goal: Prove the agent is good and safe enough to launch.
agenda.opener: How do you know this agent is good enough to put in front of customers?

evidence.strong: A suite of hundreds of scripted scenarios run against a sandboxed order system with a simulated customer, each repeated several times, graded on outcomes (correct refund, no unauthorised action), policy compliance, tone and handoff; zero tolerance for unauthorised actions; plus shadow mode on real traffic.

misconceptions.challenge: The agent passes a refund scenario once. Would it pass it ten times out of ten?

probes: How do you test refunds without real money?
What result blocks a launch outright?
hints: A fake order system lets you test actions.
agenda.moveOnSummary: Simulated scenarios against a sandbox, repeated trials, outcome and policy grading, zero unauthorised actions, and shadow mode.

agenda.goal: Hand off and get approvals without losing context.
agenda.opener: When does the agent hand over to a human, and what does that human see?

evidence.strong: Triggers: customer asks, repeated failures, detected frustration, policy-required cases, budget exhaustion; the human gets a concise summary, verified identity, actions taken and a suggested next step; large refunds go to an approval queue with one-click decisions, and the conversation resumes with the result.
evidence.adequate: Transfers the transcript to a human.

misconceptions.pattern: Thinks passing the raw transcript is enough.
misconceptions.challenge: A human agent gets a forty-message transcript. How long before they can help?

probes: How does a refund approval reach a human and come back?
hints: Approvals are a queue with an answer.
agenda.moveOnSummary: Clear escalation triggers, a summary with identity, actions and next step, and an approval queue that resumes the conversation.

agenda.goal: Make retries and repeated tool calls safe.
agenda.opener: The refund API times out and the agent tries again. What prevents a double refund?

evidence.strong: Idempotency keys per intended action passed to write tools, the refund service deduplicating on them, the agent checking state before retrying, repeated-action detection in the loop, and outcomes verified in the system of record.
evidence.adequate: Retries with a check of the order status.

misconceptions.pattern: Assumes a timeout means the refund didn't happen.
misconceptions.challenge: The refund succeeded but the response was lost. What does a blind retry do?

probes: Where does the idempotency key come from?
How does the agent confirm the refund really happened?
hints: The same intended action should map to the same key.
Check the system of record, not the model's memory.
agenda.moveOnSummary: Idempotency keys on writes, deduplication in the refund service, state checks before retries, and outcome verification.

agenda.goal: Control cost and latency per conversation.
agenda.opener: What does a conversation cost, and how do you keep it in check?

evidence.strong: Estimates tokens per turn for workflows versus agent turns and cost per resolved conversation compared with a human contact, uses a small model for routing, caches the stable system prompt and tool definitions, caps steps and tokens per conversation, and measures latency per turn.

misconceptions.challenge: A cheap conversation that ends in a human handoff anyway: was it cheap?

probes: What's the right unit to measure cost in?
Where does an agent waste tokens?
hints: Long tool outputs and extra steps add up.
agenda.moveOnSummary: Cost per resolved conversation, small-model routing, cached prompts, step and token caps, and latency per turn.

agenda.goal: Plan a staged rollout and ongoing monitoring.
agenda.opener: How would you roll this out, and what would you watch once it's live?

evidence.strong: Shadow mode drafting replies for humans, then read-only answers, then low-risk actions, then small refunds, widening limits with evidence; monitors resolution, satisfaction, handoff reasons, blocked unauthorised attempts, refunds versus policy and cost, with every conversation traced.
evidence.adequate: A gradual rollout without stages tied to risk.

probes: What's the first thing the agent is allowed to do on its own?
Which metric would make you roll back?
agenda.moveOnSummary: Shadow, then read-only, then low-risk actions, then small refunds, with resolution, satisfaction, policy and cost monitoring.

curveballs.prompt: Logs show three customers got the same refund twice yesterday after the refund service had a slow hour. What went wrong?
A customer is furious, has asked three times for a person, and the agent keeps offering help articles. What should have happened?

alternatives.choice: A single agent with all tools and no workflows
alternatives.whenBetter: When conversations are mostly unpredictable and volume is low enough that cost and variability matter less.

alternatives.choice: Multiple specialist agents with handoffs (billing, shipping, account)
alternatives.whenBetter: When tool sets and permissions differ greatly between areas and teams own them separately.

alternatives.choice: Agent-assist only, where the AI drafts replies for human agents
alternatives.whenBetter: As a first phase or in highly regulated settings where autonomous actions aren't acceptable.

exemplars.label: Bounded agent with earned authority
exemplars.outline: Clarifies volume, allowed actions and the refund limit, logged-in identity, handoff and success metrics. Routes intents to workflows and the long tail to an agent loop with retrieval over help articles and narrow typed tools behind a policy layer that takes identity from the session and enforces limits in code. Large refunds go to an approval queue; handoff passes a summary, identity and actions taken. Writes carry idempotency keys. Evaluates with repeated simulated scenarios against a sandbox and zero tolerance for unauthorised actions, tracks cost per resolution, and rolls out from shadow to read-only to small refunds.

exemplars.label: Capable but trusting agent
exemplars.outline: Builds one agent with retrieval and tools that can look up orders and refund, with refund rules in the system prompt, a transcript handoff and manual testing of a few dozen chats.

exemplars.label: FAQ bot
exemplars.outline: Pastes help articles into a prompt and answers questions; no actions, identity handling, handoff or evaluation.
